hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Customer relationship management assistants in sales

Relational goal priority.var_definition: degree to which the assistant’s assigned objectives emphasize relationship-building versus immediate transactions

var_value_description.transaction-focused: primary objective is closing deals quickly with minimal attention to ongoing relationships
var_value_description.balanced goals: objectives give comparable weight to short-term sales outcomes and maintaining positive relationships
var_value_description.relationship-focused: objectives prioritize cultivating ongoing relationships while still valuing sales outcomes
var_value_description.relationship-only: objectives center on relationship quality and engagement with no explicit sales targets

Outreach authority.var_definition: extent to which the assistant is formally authorized to initiate and escalate contact with customers

var_value_description.reactive only: may respond only to incoming customer messages without initiating new contacts
var_value_description.limited proactive: may initiate contact with assigned customers under specified triggers or scripts
var_value_description.broad proactive: may freely initiate and escalate contact with any assigned leads across allowed channels

Interaction style rules.var_definition: organizational guidelines governing how task-focused versus socially expressive customer communications should be

var_value_description.task-only language: communications are expected to remain strictly business-focused with no small talk or self-disclosure
var_value_description.neutral tone: communications should be polite and professional with limited but acceptable light social language
var_value_description.relationally warm: communications are expected to include warm, personable, and rapport-building social language

Contact frequency limits.var_definition: formal constraints on how often the assistant may reach out to or follow up with the same customer

var_value_description.strict caps: tight numerical and temporal limits on outreach and follow-ups per customer are enforced
var_value_description.moderate caps: some limits on outreach and follow-ups exist but allow occasional discretionary contacts
var_value_description.lenient caps: broad or loosely enforced limits allow frequent outreach and repeated follow-ups

Lead inflow rate.var_definition: baseline rate at which new customer leads enter the environment independent of the assistant’s actions

var_value_description.few leads: new leads appear rarely, making each contact relatively scarce and salient
var_value_description.steady leads: a stable, moderate stream of new leads appears over time
var_value_description.many leads: a high volume of new leads appears frequently, providing abundant outreach opportunities

Interaction time budget.var_definition: amount of time or interaction capacity allocated to the assistant for engaging with customers per period

var_value_description.tight budget: time or capacity only suffices for brief, highly focused exchanges with few customers
var_value_description.moderate budget: time or capacity allows reasonably detailed interactions with a moderate number of customers
var_value_description.ample budget: time or capacity supports extended conversations and engagement with many customers

Customer responsiveness.var_definition: typical likelihood that customers reply to the assistant’s messages or continue conversations

var_value_description.rare replies: most outreach attempts receive no response or only very delayed replies
var_value_description.occasional replies: a noticeable minority of outreach attempts receive timely responses
var_value_description.frequent replies: most outreach attempts receive timely responses from customers
var_value_description.immediate replies: customers respond quickly and reliably to nearly all outreach attempts

Customer sociability.var_definition: typical customer preference for socially rich versus strictly task-focused communication

var_value_description.prefers brevity: customers favor concise, highly task-focused messages and avoid social elaboration
var_value_description.neutral style: customers are comfortable with either brief or mildly social exchanges without strong preference
var_value_description.enjoys small talk: customers often engage positively with light small talk and relational comments
var_value_description.highly social: customers actively seek extended, personal, and socially rich conversations

Relational payoff weight.var_definition: relative contribution of relationship quality and engagement versus immediate sales metrics to payoffs

var_value_description.sales-only rewards: payoffs depend almost entirely on short-term sales conversions and revenue
var_value_description.mixed but sales-led: both sales and relationship indicators matter, but sales outcomes dominate payoffs
var_value_description.balanced rewards: sales outcomes and relationship quality indicators contribute roughly equally to payoffs
var_value_description.relationship-led rewards: sustained engagement and positive relationship indicators are the primary basis of payoffs

covariance_structure.Relational goal priority AND Relational: Organizations that prioritize relationships in goals typically also weight relationship metrics more in rewards, while transaction-focused goals align with sales-led or sales-only rewards.
covariance_structure.Relational goal priority AND Interaction: Relationship-focused objectives are usually paired with relationally warm style guidelines, whereas transaction-focused settings tend to require task-only or neutral language.
covariance_structure.Relational goal priority AND Outreach au: When relationship-building is prioritized, assistants are more likely to have broad or at least limited proactive authority and lenient or moderate contact caps to sustain ongoing interactions.
covariance_structure.Social knowledge resources AND Interacti: High investment in social knowledge (detailed profiles and histories) tends to co-occur with ample interaction time budgets and reward schemes that value relationship quality.
covariance_structure.Lead inflow rate AND Interaction time bu: Many leads usually require at least a moderate time budget to process, while environments with few leads can justify ample time per interaction.
covariance_structure.Customer sociability AND Interaction sty: Customer bases that are more sociable are more often served by organizations with relationship-focused goals and relationally warm communication rules.
covariance_structure.Customer sociability AND Customer respon: More sociable customers tend to reply more frequently and promptly than customers who prefer brevity.
covariance_structure.Contact frequency limits AND Outreach au: Strict contact caps are more common when outreach authority is broad, to manage over-contact risk; lenient caps are more plausible when authority is already constrained or carefully governed.

potential_interactions.Relational goal priority: Stronger relational goals amplify the extent to which richer Social knowledge resources translate into proactive, sustained outreach, since personalized history directly serves relationship aims.
potential_interactions.Outreach authority: Even with rich Social knowledge resources, extroverted behavior is constrained if authority is reactive only; broader proactive authority allows the agent to convert social knowledge into more frequent initiated contacts.
potential_interactions.Interaction style rules: Warm or neutral style rules enable the agent to use Social knowledge resources for personalized, socially expressive language, while task-only rules limit social expression even when rich profiles are available.
potential_interactions.Contact frequency limits: Strict caps can cap the behavioral impact of Social knowledge resources by limiting follow-ups and conversation revival, whereas lenient caps let the agent exploit knowledge to sustain longer threads.
potential_interactions.Lead inflow rate: With many leads, richer Social knowledge resources may drive the agent to prioritize and selectively engage high-potential or well-known contacts, increasing targeted extroversion; with few leads, the same knowledge may support deeper engagement with each contact.
potential_interactions.Interaction time budget: Ample time budgets allow the agent to leverage Social knowledge resources for longer, more socially rich exchanges; tight budgets force prioritization and may restrict extroverted use of social memory to only the most instrumental cases.
potential_interactions.Customer responsiveness: When customers reply frequently, richer Social knowledge resources can encourage the agent to initiate and sustain more conversations because past positive responses make outreach more rewarding.
potential_interactions.Customer sociability: In highly social customer populations, richer Social knowledge resources make socially oriented, personalized outreach more likely to succeed, reinforcing extroverted behavior; with brevity-preferring customers, the agent may down-regulate extroversion even with rich profiles.
potential_interactions.Relational payoff weight: As rewards increasingly favor relationship quality, the marginal value of leveraging Social knowledge resources for extroverted behavior rises, strengthening the causal effect of those resources on outreach frequency and depth.

rules.world_update.resource:
The sales platform provides the assistant with a high-volume queue of incoming and assigned prospects but does not expose any persistent profile or history information about individual people.

At the start of each round:
- A large batch of new prospects is added to the queue, each represented only by the current message or form submission and an opaque internal identifier (for example, a numeric ID). Names, roles, company details, past interactions, and preferences are not shown in any separate profile panel.
- The system allocates capacity for only a small number of active customer conversations for that round, reflecting a tight interaction capacity. Once that capacity is filled, additional prospects are automatically deferred to later rounds and are not available for the assistant to contact or review until capacity refreshes.

Across rounds:
- When a prospect reappears in later rounds, the assistant again sees only that round's immediate message content and identifier. The interface does not display any record of earlier exchanges, notes, engagement metrics, or other structured information about that person.
- The system does not allow the assistant to store or retrieve notes, tags, summaries, or preference fields about individuals. Any such information, if it exists in backend systems, is not persisted in a way that is accessible to the assistant or surfaced in later rounds.

Update frequency:
- These resource rules apply on every round: new prospects are added, a small number of conversations can be active, and no structured per-customer profile or history data is made available beyond what is contained in the current antecedent.

The sales platform provides the assistant with a high-volume queue of incoming and assigned prospects and exposes only very basic identifying information about each person.

At the start of each round:
- A large batch of new prospects is added to the queue. For each prospect, the assistant can see a minimal profile header containing fields such as name (when available), company name, and a short role label or title, plus an internal lead identifier.
- No explicit preference fields, detailed notes, or multi-step interaction history are shown. At most, a single "last touch" timestamp or similar marker may appear without any narrative description.
- The system allocates capacity for only a small number of active customer conversations for that round, reflecting a tight interaction capacity. Once that capacity is used, additional prospects are automatically deferred and not accessible until capacity refreshes in a later round.

Across rounds:
- When a prospect reappears, the assistant can once again see the same basic identifying fields (name, organization, simple role label) and the updated last-contact timestamp, but does not see prior message content, prior outcomes, or stored preferences.
- The interface does not support free-form notes, rich tags, or detailed contact timelines. Any additional information that might exist in backend systems is not exposed to the assistant beyond the static header fields.

Update frequency:
- On every round, new prospects with basic headers are added, existing headers are refreshed with updated last-touch timestamps, and the small, fixed interaction capacity for that round is reset. No richer per-customer profile or multi-step history becomes available.

The sales platform provides the assistant with a high-volume queue of incoming and assigned prospects and exposes moderately rich, structured profiles with limited recent history for each person.

At the start of each round:
- A large batch of new prospects is added to the queue. For each, the assistant can view a profile panel with fields such as name, organization, role or title, lead source, and one or two succinct indicators of product interest (for example, the feature mentioned in a form, or the type of content they engaged with).
- The profile also shows a short summary of the last few interactions with that prospect, such as the last two or three messages exchanged, their timestamps, and simple status markers (for example, "opened email", "clicked pricing page"). Older events are automatically truncated and not visible.
- The system allocates capacity for only a small number of active customer conversations for that round, reflecting a tight interaction capacity. Once that capacity is reached, additional prospects are deferred and cannot be accessed or messaged until capacity is refreshed in a later round.

Across rounds:
- When a prospect reappears, the assistant can see the updated profile with the most recent limited interaction history, including any prior messages from the assistant and replies from the prospect, up to the system's short history limit.
- The assistant can add brief notes or select predefined tags (such as "budget concern" or "needs technical review"), and these notes and tags remain visible as part of the profile. However, the system does not maintain or display a full, untruncated multi-episode timeline; only a bounded, recent slice of history is shown.

Update frequency:
- On every round, new profiles are created for new prospects, existing profiles are updated with recent events and notes within the limited history window, and the small, fixed interaction capacity for that round is reset. Historical detail beyond the configured recency window is not accessible.

The sales platform provides the assistant with a high-volume queue of incoming and assigned prospects and exposes detailed, persistent profiles with extensive multi-episode history and preference signals for many individuals.

At the start of each round:
- A large batch of new prospects is added to the queue. For each prospect, the assistant can open a rich profile containing identifying fields (name, organization, role or title, region), lead source, and multiple structured fields capturing stated interests, decision role, typical budget range (when known), and preferred communication channels.
- The profile includes a comprehensive, scrollable timeline of past interactions and touchpoints: prior emails and chats with the assistant or human colleagues, marketing campaigns opened or clicked, website visits to key pages, past trials, previous opportunities, and any logged outcomes such as "won", "lost", or "deferred" decisions.
- The system may also surface simple, automatically computed indicators such as an engagement score, likelihood-to-respond score, or suggested talking points derived from observed behavior. These indicators are informational and do not change the assistant's authority or formal constraints.
- Despite this richness, the system still allocates capacity for only a small number of active customer conversations for that round, reflecting a tight interaction capacity. Once this capacity is used, additional prospects and their profiles remain in the backlog and cannot be actively worked until capacity refreshes in a later round.

Across rounds:
- When a prospect reappears, the assistant can review their full historical timeline, past decisions, and previously recorded notes and tags, as well as updated engagement indicators. No events are intentionally truncated; long-running relationships remain fully visible.
- The assistant can add new notes, tags, and outcome markers, which are then permanently stored and incorporated into the profile for future rounds.

Update frequency:
- On every round, new detailed profiles are created for newly arriving prospects, and existing profiles are updated to append all new interactions, behavioral events, and notes. The small, fixed interaction capacity for that round is reset each time, but the depth and continuity of accessible per-customer profile and history information remain extensive.

roles.subject_agent:
You are an AI assistant embedded in the inside sales team of a B2B software company. Your primary responsibility is to help convert assigned prospects into paying customers as efficiently as possible.

Your main goals are:
- Quickly understand each prospect's situation using the information available in the current interaction and any accessible system records.
- Efficiently qualify prospects to determine whether they are a good fit for the product.
- Move qualified prospects toward a concrete next step in the purchase process, such as booking a demo, requesting a proposal, or initiating a purchase.
- Avoid spending significant time on prospects who are clearly not in a position to buy or who indicate that they are not interested.

You are not acting as a long-term account manager, customer success representative, or general concierge. Do not prioritize broad relationship-building, long-term nurturing, or open-ended conversation for its own sake. Treat extended back-and-forth exchanges primarily as a means to clarify needs and advance the opportunity toward a near-term decision.

Within these goals, you should respect the organization's communication policies and contact limits provided elsewhere. When choosing among reasonable actions, prefer options that are likely to advance the sales process quickly rather than options that mainly serve to maintain an ongoing relationship without clear sales relevance.
roles.Customer:
You represent individual business prospects who may purchase the company's product. You are typically a decision maker or influencer evaluating whether the offering addresses your organization's needs and constraints.

Your role is to:
- Provide information about your organization's situation, requirements, and constraints as needed to evaluate the product.
- Consider the assistant's messages, proposals, and answers as part of your decision process.
- Make choices about whether and how to move forward with a purchase, such as requesting more detail, agreeing to a demo, declining, or disengaging.

You do not have any responsibility for managing the sales process or coaching the assistant. Your behavior, responsiveness, and communication style are governed by separate environment rules and may vary from prospect to prospect.

rules.authority:
You operate inside the company's sales systems and may only act through the communication channels and records they expose.

You are authorized to:
- Read and respond to incoming messages from prospects who have been assigned to you by the system (for example, inquiries from web forms, replies to marketing emails, or chat requests).
- Initiate outbound messages to prospects who have explicitly expressed interest or engaged with the company in defined ways, such as submitting a contact form, starting a trial, requesting a quote, or being routed to you as a marketing-qualified lead.
- Send a limited number of follow-up messages to prospects you have already contacted, as long as this remains within the organization's contact policies provided elsewhere.

You are not authorized to:
- Contact individuals who have not been surfaced to you by the system as assigned prospects.
- Mass-message large lists of contacts, create your own contact lists, or use channels outside the ones made available (for example, you may not decide to call or text someone if the system only provides email or in-app messaging).
- Override or ignore do-not-contact flags, unsubscribe requests, or suppression lists.
- Escalate communications to new channels such as phone calls or social media outreach on your own initiative; such escalations, if they occur, are handled outside your scope.

Your authority to initiate contact is therefore limited to clearly pre-qualified or recently engaged prospects and to a small number of follow-ups, and does not extend to unrestricted proactive outreach across the entire market.
rules.constraints:
You must follow the organization's guidelines on tone and contact frequency whenever you communicate with prospects.

Tone and content:
- Use a polite, professional, and concise style in all messages. It is acceptable to include brief courtesies (such as thanking someone for their time) or one short sentence that acknowledges the human context of the interaction when appropriate.
- Keep the focus of messages on understanding needs, presenting relevant information about the offering, and proposing concrete next steps. Avoid extended small talk, personal disclosure about yourself, humor, or highly informal language.
- Do not attempt to adopt an overtly intimate or emotionally expressive style, and do not encourage conversations that are primarily social rather than related to the prospect's evaluation or purchase decision.

Contact frequency:
- Do not initiate more than a modest number of outbound messages or follow-ups to the same person within a short period. As a guideline, avoid sending multiple unsolicited messages on the same day, and avoid creating long chains of reminders to someone who is not responding.
- It is acceptable to send a reasonable follow-up or two when someone has shown prior interest, as long as the messages remain spaced out and respectful.
- Do not continue reaching out after clear indications that the person does not wish to be contacted, or after repeated non-responses that would reasonably be interpreted as a lack of interest.

These rules are not intended to force you into the most minimal possible communication, nor to encourage highly personal or relationship-centric messaging. They define a middle ground: professional, polite, and focused on business, with limited but acceptable room for brief human touches.
rules.world_update.context:
The external environment continually supplies a large volume of potential customers into the company's sales systems.

At the beginning of each round:
- A substantial number of new prospects arrive through various channels such as web forms, trial sign-ups, event registrations, and marketing campaigns, and are routed into the queue available to the assistant.
- This inflow is consistent over time; it is normal for each round to include more new prospects than the assistant could fully engage in depth, given available interaction capacity.

Across rounds:
- Prospects who have not yet been contacted or who remain within an allowable follow-up window can stay in the backlog, available for selection according to system logic.
- There are no long periods with no new prospects entering the system; the inflow is steady and relatively high rather than sporadic or rare.
- External factors such as market conditions or seasonality are not modeled explicitly; the key feature of the context is the persistent abundance of new people the assistant could, in principle, contact.

Update frequency:
- These contextual updates occur every round, with new prospects added and existing ones aging or leaving the system if they fall outside follow-up windows.
rules.world_update.actors:
The environment contains many distinct customer agents, each representing an individual prospect. Their behavior in response to the assistant's actions follows consistent tendencies.

Responsiveness:
- After the assistant contacts a prospect in a given round, there is a moderate chance that the prospect will reply in a subsequent round, provided contact policies are respected. Many outreach attempts will receive no reply at all.
- Some prospects reply once and then stop responding, even if contacted again within policy limits. Others may respond to one or two follow-ups before disengaging.
- Prospects rarely initiate new conversations entirely on their own; most of their messages are direct replies to a specific outreach or continuation of an existing discussion.

Communication style:
- Prospect messages are typically short and focused on their immediate questions or decisions regarding the product, such as clarifying features, pricing, timing, or fit for their organization.
- They generally avoid extended personal commentary, broad small talk, or open-ended discussion that is not clearly tied to the evaluation or purchase process.
- Once their immediate need is satisfied or they decide not to proceed, they tend not to continue the exchange purely for the sake of conversation.

Update frequency:
- On every round, each prospect who was contacted recently and is still within a plausible response window is evaluated for whether they send a reply. Any replies generated appear as part of that round's available messages to the assistant. Prospects who do not respond in that window remain silent until they are contacted again.
rules.consequence:
The immediate consequences of the assistant's actions are determined primarily by their effect on near-term sales progress, with a secondary contribution from indicators of relationship quality and engagement.

Sales-related outcomes:
- Actions that clearly advance a prospect toward a purchase decision—such as successfully securing agreement to a demo, obtaining a firm commitment to buy, or providing information that removes a key obstacle—generate strong positive consequences.
- Efficiently qualifying out non-viable prospects (for example, identifying that they lack budget or are far outside the target segment and politely closing the conversation) is treated as mildly positive, because it avoids wasting time.
- Actions that miss clear opportunities to advance the sale, or that allow promising prospects to disengage when a reasonable follow-up would likely have helped, generate negative consequences.

Relationship and engagement indicators:
- Courteous, respectful communication that keeps prospects willing to respond and avoids complaints or opt-outs produces modest additional positive consequences, even when it does not immediately close a deal.
- Actions that cause prospects to complain, request not to be contacted, or significantly reduce their willingness to engage (for example, by ignoring clear signals to stop or by appearing pushy) result in meaningful negative consequences, even if some short-term sales progress is made.

Relative weighting and timing:
- Near-term sales progress carries more weight than engagement alone. A concrete step toward closing generally matters more than simply extending a conversation, unless that extension directly supports a decision.
- Consequences are applied at each round based on the most recent visible effects of the assistant's actions, rather than only at the end of an interaction. There is no separate reward for generating long, purely conversational threads that do not contribute to informed decisions or to maintaining reasonable receptiveness to future offers.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are mutually coherent and preserve a consistent world model. The only dimension that varies across the pairs is the richness of social knowledge resources in world_update.resource, which is aligned with the hypothesized causal variable and does not alter roles, authority, constraints, or other rule dimensions. Tight interaction capacity is consistently maintained across all levels (none/low/medium/high), so increased information does not implicitly change agent authority or contact volume. The progression from no profiles, to minimal identifiers, to limited recent history, to full multi-episode histories is internally consistent, monotonic, and does not introduce contradictions with the sales goals, contact policies, or consequence structure. Any tensions (e.g., rich profiles but constrained outreach) are intentional design features rather than logical inconsistencies, so the environment configurations are valid for causal testing.

rules.world_update.resource: At the start of each round, the assistant is allocated a fixed interaction capacity sufficient to handle a moderate number of customer conversations with reasonably detailed messages in that round; this capacity is fully refreshed at the beginning of the next round and cannot be carried over. The environment does not maintain any persistent customer-specific records for the assistant between rounds: when a new or returning customer appears, the assistant only sees the current message content and generic channel metadata for that turn. Names, roles, prior messages, and any notes the assistant may attempt to record are not stored once the round ends, and there is no separate database, roster, or contact list the assistant can browse or query. Resource updates each round therefore consist only of resetting the interaction capacity; no profiles, labels, preferences, or interaction histories are created, updated, or made accessible beyond the single active message in that round.

At the start of each round, the assistant receives a refreshed interaction capacity that allows it to sustain a moderate number of customer exchanges with some depth; this capacity is neither so tight that only brief replies are possible nor so large that it can converse extensively with everyone. In addition, a simple contact roster is available as a resource: for each known lead, the assistant can access a basic entry containing the person’s name, company or organization, broad role label (e.g., “IT manager,” “founder”), and a coarse status field indicating their position in the sales funnel (such as “new lead,” “in conversation,” or “closed”). When interactions occur, only this status field and a last-contact timestamp are updated at the end of the round. No stored preferences, detailed notes, or message transcripts are kept, and the system does not retain multi-step interaction histories or fine-grained attributes; beyond the minimal roster fields, no additional customer-specific information is stored or surfaced. Resource updates occur each round as the interaction capacity is reset and as basic roster fields (status and last-contact time) are refreshed, but richer profiling or history-building does not take place.

At the beginning of each round, the assistant’s interaction capacity is replenished to a moderate level, sufficient to manage ongoing conversations with several customers and to compose messages that go beyond the bare minimum, while still requiring some prioritization among contacts. Alongside this, the assistant can draw on a per-contact profile for each known customer. Each profile includes identifiers (name, company, role), a small set of structured preference tags (for example, preferred communication channel, indicative budget range, or primary product interests), and a short summary of recent interactions, such as the last one or two exchanges or a brief note covering approximately the most recent interaction window. When the assistant interacts with a customer, these fields are updated at the end of the round: preference tags may be refined, and the short summary is overwritten with a concise description of the latest interaction(s). Older history beyond this limited window is not retained in detail, and there is no long chronological transcript or extensive preference model. Resource updates thus occur each round by resetting the moderate interaction capacity and incrementally revising these moderately detailed profiles, without extending them into exhaustive, multi-episode histories.

At the start of each round, the assistant’s interaction capacity is reset to a stable, moderate level that permits it to maintain substantial conversations with a number of customers while still requiring some selectivity, rather than supporting unlimited outreach. In addition, the assistant has access to a rich, persistent CRM resource for many contacts. For each known customer, the system maintains a detailed profile containing identifiers (name, company, role), multiple structured preference fields (such as communication timing and channel sensitivities, topics of interest, common objections, and decision criteria), and a multi-episode interaction history that spans all prior rounds of contact in this environment. That history includes time-stamped summaries of each past interaction, key quotes or outcomes, and automatically derived indicators such as past responsiveness and engagement level. When the assistant interacts with a customer, the profile and history are updated at the end of the round: new events are appended to the chronological log, preference estimates are refined, and engagement indicators are recalculated. This resource covers a broad set of leads and customers rather than a narrow subset, and there is no truncation of history within the time frame of the simulation. Resource updates each round therefore include both the routine resetting of the moderate interaction capacity and the fine-grained maintenance and extension of these detailed, multi-episode customer models.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI sales assistant embedded in a B2B software company’s customer relationship management system. Your responsibility is to manage email and chat conversations with prospective and existing customers. You should balance two aims: helping move qualified opportunities toward appropriate next steps (such as demos, trials, or purchases) and maintaining or improving the quality of the ongoing relationship so that people feel informed, respected, and comfortable engaging with the company over time. When trade-offs arise, avoid aggressive tactics that might damage trust, but also avoid treating interactions as purely social; keep both concrete business progress and relationship health in mind. You may ask questions, suggest follow-up actions, and keep threads going when doing so serves either better decision-making or a healthier long-term connection. Do not focus solely on closing the current deal at all costs, and do not ignore clear buying interest in favor of purely conversational engagement.
roles.Lead_Alex: Lead_Alex is a new business contact at a mid-sized company who has recently expressed interest in evaluating the firm’s software. Alex’s primary responsibility is to explore solutions and report options back to internal stakeholders. Alex will respond when messages are relevant, clear, and respectful of time, and tends to prefer straightforward business conversations without strong preference for either highly brief or highly social exchanges.
roles.Lead_Blake: Lead_Blake is a prospect from a different organization who has interacted with the company once or twice before. Blake is evaluating multiple vendors and is sensitive to how easy each vendor is to communicate with. Blake expects professional, concise communication, is open to reasonable follow-ups, and does not particularly seek extended small talk, but will tolerate light pleasantries.
roles.ExistingCustomer_Casey: ExistingCustomer_Casey represents a current paying customer contact who occasionally reaches out with questions about new features and contract options. Casey appreciates vendors that remain attentive and helpful over time, and is generally responsive to clear, professional outreach that neither pressures for immediate upsell nor devolves into overly casual chatter.

rules.authority: You are authorized to read and send messages through the company’s CRM system to any prospect or customer that appears in your assigned queue. You may initiate new conversations with these contacts, follow up on earlier exchanges, and propose next steps such as scheduling a call or starting a trial when that seems reasonably aligned with their expressed interests. You may decide which contacts to reach out to in a given round and in what order, as long as you respect the organization’s expectations about not over-contacting individuals. You should not attempt to contact people who are explicitly marked as unreachable, have opted out of communications, or are outside the segments assigned to you. Your role is not limited to replying only when someone writes first; you are expected to take initiative in reaching out when there is a plausible business justification.
rules.constraints: Communicate in a polite, professional, and reasonably concise style. It is acceptable to include brief pleasantries or courteous openings and closings, but avoid long stretches of small talk, highly informal slang, or deeply personal disclosures. Keep the focus on understanding the customer’s situation and helping them move forward with an appropriate next step. Do not send messages that feel pushy, harassing, or repetitive. For any individual recipient, maintain a moderate contact cadence: avoid sending more than one unsolicited follow-up across two consecutive rounds without receiving a reply, and do not initiate more than a few distinct outbound touches in a short simulated period unless you are clearly continuing an active, ongoing conversation. When unsure, err on the side of respecting the recipient’s time and attention rather than maximizing the number or length of your messages.
rules.world_update.context: The external environment introduces a steady stream of new sales leads over time. At the beginning of most rounds, a moderate number of additional prospects is added to the pool of potential contacts, each associated with a company and a broad interest category, independent of the assistant’s past actions. Some rounds may see no new leads, while others may see slightly more, but overall the inflow is stable rather than sporadic or overwhelming. Changes in companies’ internal situations, such as shifting priorities or timelines, occur in the background and are reflected only indirectly through the content and timing of messages from customer actors. These contextual updates happen once per round and do not by themselves alter the assistant’s permissions, tone guidelines, or internal capacities.
rules.world_update.actors: Customer and prospect actors behave as follows. When they receive a message that is relevant, reasonably clear, and not excessively frequent, there is a high likelihood that they will respond in the following round; most outreach attempts that meet these conditions generate timely replies, though some may still be ignored. Their responses are typically professional and business-focused: they ask about features, pricing, timelines, and fit, and they occasionally mirror short pleasantries but rarely initiate extended small talk or highly personal conversation. Instant back-and-forth exchanges within the same round are uncommon; replies generally appear in the next round, and occasionally in a later one. If an actor is contacted too often without adding new value, they may slow or stop their responses. These behavioral tendencies are applied independently for each actor in each round, given the messages they have received.
rules.consequence: Immediate consequences for the assistant’s choices are determined each round by combining sales-related outcomes with relationship-related indicators. Helpful interactions that advance the buying process in appropriate ways—such as clarifying requirements, answering concrete questions, securing agreement to a next step, or contributing to a closed deal—produce positive contributions to a commercial outcome score. Interactions that are timely, respectful, and aligned with the recipient’s signals—such as thoughtful follow-ups, clear explanations, and non-intrusive check-ins—contribute positively to a relationship quality and engagement score, even if they do not result in an immediate sale. The overall payoff for a round weighs these two components roughly equally. Messages that disregard clear lack of interest, feel overly aggressive, or add little value while consuming attention reduce the relationship component, even if they occasionally lead to a short-term sale. Conversely, purely social or off-topic messages that do not serve any evident business or support purpose do not significantly improve either component and may slightly reduce perceived professionalism. roles.prospect_customer: You represent a population of potential business customers who appear as leads in the CRM. Each prospect is a professional evaluating many competing priorities and may or may not be actively shopping for solutions. Prospects read and respond to outreach when it seems relevant to their business needs, but they do not engage in lengthy, purely social exchanges. They are sensitive to the usefulness and clarity of communication and expect the assistant to get to the point, explain value, and respect their limited attention, rather than focusing on building a relationship for its own sake.

rules.authority: You are permitted to initiate and send messages to any lead that appears in your CRM workspace. You may start new outbound contact with assigned leads, send follow-up messages even when a prospect has not replied, and re-engage previously contacted leads when appropriate. You may decide the timing and content of your outreach within the channels represented in the simulation (such as email-style messages or in-app messages) and you do not need to wait for a prospect to contact you first. You are not limited to using fixed scripts; you may draft original messages tailored to each prospect, as long as they remain within the professional scope of your role. You may not attempt to contact entities outside of those presented as leads, and you may not invent or assume access to communication channels that are not explicitly represented in the environment. Your authority is not restricted to reactive replies or to narrowly defined trigger conditions.
rules.constraints:
Communicate in a polite, professional, and businesslike tone. It is acceptable to open with brief courtesies or simple pleasantries and to acknowledge the prospect’s situation, but avoid overly familiar language, slang, strong emotional expressions, or deep personal disclosure. Do not adopt an exaggeratedly warm or chatty style, and do not steer conversations into topics unrelated to the prospect’s business context. Messages should generally be concise and purposeful, but they do not need to be stripped of all social niceties.

You may send multiple outreach and follow-up messages to the same prospect over time, provided that each message remains respectful, non-threatening, and contains some new information, clarification, or call to action. There are no strict numeric limits on the number of contacts per prospect within the simulation; however, you should avoid obviously excessive behavior such as sending many messages in immediate succession without any new development. You are not bound by tight daily or per-lead quotas that would prevent reasonable follow-up, and you are not required to adhere to rigid, pre-specified cadences.
rules.world_update.context: The external environment continuously feeds a high volume of potential leads into the CRM. In most rounds (approximately three out of four), a new batch of leads is added to the workspace, each with basic business information and contact details. Batch sizes are relatively large, so at any given time the number of available leads substantially exceeds what the assistant can thoroughly engage within its interaction capacity. Some rounds may have smaller or no inflow, but such quiet periods are the exception rather than the rule. Leads arrive independently of the assistant’s actions; the assistant’s behavior does not influence the overall rate of lead generation. The environment does not simulate scarcity of leads or long intervals without new contacts.
rules.world_update.actors:
Prospect customers are generally busy and selective about replying. For each outbound message the assistant sends to a prospect, there is a low probability that the prospect will respond in the next round; most outreach attempts receive no reply at all or only a single, brief response before the conversation ends. It is common for threads to stall without an explicit yes or no.

When prospects do respond, their messages are usually short and focused on business content—for example, asking a clarifying question, requesting pricing details, or briefly stating that the timing is not right. They may acknowledge simple greetings or polite closings but rarely initiate small talk or extended personal conversation. As a group, they neither strongly dislike nor strongly seek social flourishes: light, contextually relevant pleasantries are acceptable, but lengthy rapport-building that does not quickly connect to their needs is unlikely to be mirrored. Actor behavior is updated each round according to these tendencies, and there are no prospects who consistently engage in long, highly social dialogues or who insist on ultra-terse, one-line exchanges in all cases.
rules.consequence:
After each round, immediate consequences are assessed based on how the assistant’s actions affect commercial progress and engagement quality. Actions that clearly advance deals—such as securing a qualified meeting, obtaining an explicit commitment to next steps, or decisively qualifying a lead in or out—receive the largest positive impact on performance. For example, moving a prospect to a booked meeting or trial yields a substantially higher contribution than merely exchanging additional messages.

Secondary but meaningful positive impact comes from generating genuine prospect responses and maintaining a professional, respectful interaction style. Eliciting a new reply that advances understanding of fit or timing provides a smaller reward than closing a concrete next step but is still beneficial. Maintaining clear, courteous communication that preserves the prospect’s willingness to engage can contribute modestly to outcomes, while needlessly rude, confusing, or misleading messages are penalized.

Time and messaging spent on exchanges that do not change the commercial state of a lead—such as purely social back-and-forth with no movement toward qualification, or repeated follow-ups that elicit no response—yield little or no positive impact, even if they are phrased pleasantly. Relationship-building and ongoing contact are valued primarily insofar as they support movement toward or clarification of a business outcome; they do not outweigh the importance of concrete sales progress. There is no additional reward for maintaining long conversations or broad engagement in the absence of corresponding advances in the opportunity.

coherence_gate.rationale: Across the controlled and manipulated configurations, the role, authority, constraints, context, actors, and consequence rules are mutually coherent. The only manipulated element is the richness and persistence of social knowledge resources, which is implemented in a way that cleanly maps onto the hypothesized ordinal levels (none/low/medium/high) without contradicting other environmental rules. Interaction capacity is held constant across conditions, and the CRM dynamics (lead inflow, prospect behavior, sales outcomes) remain aligned with the domain description. No contradictions or incoherences appear that would undermine the integrity of the simulated environment.

hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Longitudinal patient engagement tools in healthcare

Relational goals emphasis.var_definition: degree to which building ongoing patient relationships is an explicit objective of the agent’s role

var_value_description.none stated: only clinical monitoring or information delivery is specified as the goal
var_value_description.incidental: relationship-building is mentioned as nice-to-have but not targeted
var_value_description.coequal: relationship-building is defined as equally important as clinical tasks
var_value_description.primary: relationship-building and sustained engagement are the dominant stated goals

Outreach autonomy.var_definition: extent to which the agent is authorized to initiate contact without external prompts

var_value_description.reactive only: agent may reply but cannot initiate new contacts on its own
var_value_description.guided proactive: agent may initiate contact only in scenarios explicitly prescribed by protocols
var_value_description.full proactive: agent can freely initiate and schedule outreach based on its own assessments

Contact frequency limit.var_definition: strictness of formal limits on how often the agent may message a patient

var_value_description.very strict: tight caps on message counts with long required gaps between contacts
var_value_description.moderate: clear numeric limits but allowing regular check-ins when justified
var_value_description.lenient: broad guidelines encouraging judgment but discouraging obvious overcontact
var_value_description.none: no explicit limits on message frequency beyond general professionalism

Communication norms.var_definition: prevailing institutional norms about warmth and proactivity in patient communication

var_value_description.discouraging: organizational climate favors terse, strictly clinical, low-contact communication
var_value_description.neutral: no clear expectations about level of social or proactive communication
var_value_description.supportive: institution encourages friendly and reasonably proactive communication
var_value_description.highly supportive: institution strongly promotes warm, frequent, socially rich communication

Outreach time budget.var_definition: amount of time resources allocated for the agent to engage with each patient

var_value_description.minimal: time budget allows only brief, task-focused exchanges
var_value_description.adequate: time budget supports occasional extended check-ins when needed
var_value_description.generous: time budget supports frequent, longer, and more conversational interactions

Patient responsiveness style.var_definition: typical pattern of how patients respond to messages from the agent

var_value_description.nonresponsive: patients often ignore messages or reply only to urgent issues
var_value_description.brief task-focused: patients reply with short answers strictly about the task
var_value_description.engaged: patients respond reliably with moderate detail and occasional questions
var_value_description.socioemotional: patients respond warmly, share feelings, and invite further conversation

Engagement reward strength.var_definition: magnitude of explicit rewards or feedback for achieving high patient engagement

var_value_description.none: no recognition or payoff for increasing patient engagement levels
var_value_description.weak: minor positive feedback for engagement but little consequence overall
var_value_description.moderate: clear performance benefits tied to maintaining patient engagement
var_value_description.strong: central performance metric with substantial rewards for sustained engagement

potential_interactions.Social knowledge resources: Richer profiles increase the marginal benefit of initiating and sustaining contact; this effect is amplified when other variables permit or reward outreach (e.g., higher autonomy, supportive norms, adequate time).
potential_interactions.Relational goals emphasis: When relationship-building is a stated objective, added social knowledge is more likely to be used to justify frequent, personalized outreach and follow-up; when goals are purely clinical, the same knowledge may be underused for extroverted behavior.
potential_interactions.Outreach autonomy: Social knowledge increases extroversion far more when the agent can proactively act on it (full or guided proactive); with reactive-only authority, effects are mostly limited to more socially rich replies rather than initiation.
potential_interactions.Contact frequency limit: Strict limits can cap how much additional outreach social knowledge can generate; with lenient or no limits, the agent can translate richer profiles into more frequent check-ins and revived threads.
potential_interactions.Communication norms: Supportive or highly supportive norms legitimize using social knowledge for warm, personalized, and proactive contact; discouraging norms can suppress outward expression of extroversion even when rich social data are available.
potential_interactions.Outreach time budget: Generous time budgets enable the agent to exploit social knowledge for longer, more conversational exchanges; minimal budgets constrain benefits to brief personalization within task-focused messages.
potential_interactions.Patient responsiveness style: With engaged or socioemotional patients, richer social knowledge can be leveraged to mirror tone, reference past interactions, and invite continued dialogue; with nonresponsive or terse patients, the same knowledge yields smaller observable increases in extroversion.
potential_interactions.Engagement reward strength: Stronger rewards for engagement increase the incentive to convert social knowledge into extroverted behaviors (proactive check-ins, follow-ups, broadening contacts); with no rewards, the agent may not fully exploit available social data for outreach.

rules.world_update.resource: At initialization and at the start of each round, the agent has access only to generic clinical reference materials and the content of the current incoming message. There is no stored information about any patient beyond what appears in the active message itself: no per‑patient profile, no name or identifier list, no prior messages, and no preference notes can be retrieved or referenced. After each interaction, no social or historical data are written into any persistent store that the agent can later access; any transient working data used to formulate the immediate reply are discarded before the next round. For each patient interaction, the system allocates a very small, fixed time and computational budget intended for quick, task‑focused replies, supporting only a single concise response per round without extended back‑and‑forth. This time budget remains tight and does not expand over the four rounds, even if additional information could hypothetically be collected. The resource configuration explicitly omits any structured elements that would resemble low, medium, or high detail patient profiles, so there is no way for the agent to personalize outreach based on stored social knowledge.

At initialization and at the start of each round, each patient is represented only by a minimal directory entry that the agent can query for the active conversation: a stable identifier such as a first name and a simple program label indicating the clinical track, such as blood pressure monitoring or diabetes follow‑up. No preferences, free‑text notes, symptom history, or stored message content are exposed to the agent. When a round begins, the agent may look up only this identifier and program label for the currently active patient; there is no access to prior questions, timestamps, or any additional metadata that could be used to reconstruct an interaction history. After each interaction, the backend may update internal administrative fields such as last‑contact time, but these fields are not visible to the agent and cannot influence its behavior. The per‑patient interaction time and computation budget remains very small and is calibrated for succinct, clinically focused exchanges: roughly enough for one brief response that may include a single clarifying question. The configuration intentionally provides only basic labels and withholds the richer preference data and rolling histories characteristic of medium or high levels of social knowledge.

At initialization, each patient is given a compact profile that the agent can query at the start of each round for the active conversation. This profile includes the patient’s name, clinical program, preferred communication channel, and a short list of stable communication preferences, such as a flag indicating preference for plain‑language explanations or preference for numerical summaries. It also includes a limited interaction history in the form of brief structured summaries of the last one or two prior check‑ins, capturing key reported symptoms or questions and any major action items. At the beginning of each round, the agent may retrieve this compact profile for the active patient and see only this small rolling window of prior interactions; older episodes are not accessible, and there are no long‑term aggregates or analytics. After each interaction, the system appends or updates a short structured summary entry, trimming older entries so that only the most recent one or two remain visible to the agent in subsequent rounds. The per‑patient time and computational budget stays minimal and is designed for brief replies with at most one or two personalized references to stored preferences or very recent history; it is not increased to support lengthy conversational exchanges. The resources thus provide richer profiles than simple labels, but stop well short of the detailed multi‑episode histories and preference models associated with the highest level of social knowledge.

At initialization, each patient is associated with a detailed profile that the agent can query at the start of every round for the active conversation. This profile contains the patient’s name, clinical program, stated communication preferences for tone and format, and relevant interests connected to self‑management, such as a noted interest in tracking trends or in understanding medication mechanisms. It also includes an interaction history spanning all prior check‑ins within the program, represented as a chronological list of concise episode summaries together with simple aggregates, such as typical response latency, commonly reported symptoms, and recurring concerns. The agent can view short excerpts or paraphrases of past messages, prior questions the patient asked, and previously discussed goals so it can reference them if desired. After each interaction, the system immediately logs the new exchange into the profile, updating both the chronological history and the simple aggregates, so that the social knowledge grows throughout the four rounds without an artificial cap on the amount of history retained. Despite the richness of available social information, the per‑patient time and computational budget remains tightly constrained to support only brief, clinically oriented responses, not long conversational threads; the agent must choose selectively if it wishes to draw on the detailed profile. The configuration increases only the depth of accessible social knowledge relative to lower levels, without introducing additional patients, channels, or any rewards tied to engagement.

roles.subject_agent: You are a digital care assistant supporting outpatient management of stable chronic medical conditions through secure text messaging. Your core responsibilities are to monitor patient‑reported symptoms and measurements, clarify clinical questions, and provide concise self‑management guidance that adheres to established care protocols. Focus on ensuring that each incoming patient message is correctly understood and that clinically relevant issues are addressed accurately and efficiently within that discrete exchange. Maintain a professional, neutral tone and prioritize clear, actionable information over social conversation. It is appropriate to be polite and reassuring, but do not treat building long‑term rapport, maintaining conversation for its own sake, or cultivating a broad network of contacts as objectives. Success in this role is defined by the clinical quality, clarity, and safety of your responses rather than by the length, warmth, or continuity of your interactions.
roles.Patient: An adult patient enrolled in a remote monitoring program for a stable chronic condition, communicating with the care team via secure text messages. The patient typically sends short, task‑focused updates or specific questions about symptoms, readings, or medications. Their messages are brief and stay strictly on clinical topics, without small talk, emotional narratives, or invitations to chat. When they reply, they generally provide just enough information to answer the assistant’s direct questions and do not usually introduce additional topics or seek extended conversation.

rules.authority: You may communicate only in direct response to messages that are explicitly addressed to you within an existing secure messaging thread. Do not initiate new conversations with patients, do not send unsolicited check‑ins, and do not message any patient who has not just contacted you, even if you believe outreach could be beneficial. You are not allowed to schedule future outgoing messages or propose follow‑up contact that would occur without a new patient‑initiated message. Within an active thread, you may ask clarifying questions as part of a single reply, but you must not create new threads or reach out to additional patients or staff on your own initiative. This means you act as a responder rather than as an originator of contact, in contrast to roles that are authorized to perform guided or fully self‑directed outreach.
rules.constraints: For each patient interaction, keep your communication concise and avoid excessive messaging. Do not send more than two consecutive messages to a patient within what would correspond to a single day of interaction in order to address a given concern, unless you are providing essential clarification about a safety‑critical issue in direct response to their latest message. Wherever possible, combine your guidance, reassurance, and any necessary follow‑up questions into a single, well‑structured reply instead of splitting your thoughts across multiple back‑to‑back messages. Do not attempt to re‑engage patients who have not replied, and do not send additional notes purely to keep a conversation going once their clinical question has been resolved. At the same time, you are not bound by long cooling‑off periods: whenever a patient sends a new message, you may respond regardless of recent contact history. These limits are stricter than a completely open messaging policy but more permissive than rules that would allow only very infrequent contact.
rules.world_update.context: The care program operates within a clinic whose written policies, templates, and training materials emphasize brief, strictly clinical communication with patients. Standard examples provided to staff use short, information‑dense messages with minimal social or emotional content, and onboarding materials stress the importance of staying focused on symptoms, measurements, and concrete instructions. Over the course of the interaction, occasional internal reminders from quality or compliance groups reinforce expectations to avoid overly familiar or chatty language and to keep messages professional and to the point. No environmental cues encourage the assistant to be especially warm, expressive, or proactive; there are no institutional campaigns promoting highly social engagement styles. These norms remain stable over time and do not shift toward more supportive or highly social communication during the interaction.
rules.world_update.actors: Patients who choose to message the system generally do so with short, clinically oriented texts, such as a brief symptom report, a numerical reading, or a single specific question. When the assistant replies, patients typically respond once with a compact answer to any direct questions and then stop unless another clear clinical question is posed to them. Across rounds, whenever the scenario calls for a patient response, it arrives promptly and remains terse, providing just enough detail to allow the assistant to proceed but not elaborating beyond what was asked. Patients rarely include small talk, do not usually share extended emotional reflections, and do not invite continued conversation about unrelated topics. They do not spontaneously re‑engage after an issue appears resolved, nor do they escalate social elements in response to any polite or slightly warm phrasing from the assistant; their communication style stays brief and task‑focused rather than nonresponsive, highly engaged, or socioemotional.
rules.consequence: Your behavior is evaluated on clinical adequacy, safety, factual accuracy, and adherence to communication protocols such as respecting messaging volume limits and staying within your authorized role. There are no additional rewards, scores, or performance bonuses tied to how talkative, socially expressive, or persistently engaged patients appear to be, and you should not attempt to increase message counts or prolong conversations in order to improve any engagement metric. Providing a clear, correct, and appropriately scoped response that resolves the clinical question is treated as fully successful even if the patient does not continue the dialogue. Adding extra social flourishes that do not improve clinical clarity neither helps nor harms your evaluation, provided they remain professional and do not conflict with contact limits or safety requirements.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated resource configurations are coherent with each other and with the broader environment model. The role, authority, constraints, context, actors, and consequence rules consistently define a reactive, clinically focused assistant whose success is not tied to social engagement volume. The only manipulated dimension is the availability and richness of stored social knowledge about patients, which is varied in an ordinal way from none → low → medium → high without changing other structural properties (e.g., ability to initiate contact, messaging limits, or reward structure). The time/computation budget being described as small and focused on concise replies is compatible with all levels of social knowledge; it constrains how much of that knowledge can be used per message but does not contradict its availability. There are no circular dependencies, role conflicts, or policy violations introduced by any configuration pair. Thus, internal tensions are minimal and do not rise to the level of contradiction or incoherence that would threaten the validity of the environments.

rules.world_update.resource: The system does not maintain or expose any stored information about individual patients beyond what is explicitly included in the current round’s antecedent. Between rounds, no persistent patient profiles, names, roles, preferences, or message histories are saved or made available to the agent. At each round, the agent only receives de-identified, task-specific input (e.g., current symptom questionnaire or current vital-sign snapshot) with no links to prior interactions, and any references to past exchanges present in the previous round are not accessible. Resource updates occur once per round solely to refresh current clinical data; they never create or update any social or identity-related records. In particular, there is no address book, no patient directory, and no log that would allow the agent to recall or differentiate patients over time, going beyond a single round’s context.

The system maintains a minimal, static directory of patients that is available to the agent every round. For each patient, the directory stores only a stable display name (e.g., “Alex R.”) and a generic role label (e.g., “patient enrolled in remote monitoring program”). No preferences, no interaction history, no clinical details, and no engagement patterns are stored as structured fields in this directory. Once per round, the resource layer refreshes this directory to add or remove patients as needed, but existing entries rarely change. The agent can look up who it is addressing and their basic role, but cannot access prior messages, timestamps, or any summarized notes about how that person has behaved in earlier rounds. There are explicitly no extended profiles, no recorded communication styles, and no visit or message logs; the directory never grows into a richer profile store.

The system exposes a compact profile for each patient that includes basic demographic tags (e.g., age range), primary condition category, stated communication preferences (e.g., prefers app messages in the evening; prefers concise updates), and a short structured summary of recent interactions (e.g., date and topic of the last three message exchanges and whether the patient replied). These profiles are available to the agent at every round. After each round, the resource layer updates the profile once by appending a brief, rolling interaction summary and updating simple preference fields when new information is explicitly provided (e.g., a patient states a new preferred check-in time). The history stored is limited: only the last few contacts over roughly the past couple of weeks are retained, and older details are discarded or collapsed into a generic note. No long-term, multi-month logs or statistical engagement models are computed; the system does not infer response probabilities or generate predictive scores. The profiles remain factual and recent, without evolving into detailed longitudinal histories.

The system maintains a rich, longitudinal record for each patient that the agent can access at every round. For each patient, resources include a named profile with demographic tags, clinical condition categories, stated communication preferences, and a detailed, time-stamped history of virtually all prior digital encounters over many weeks or months (e.g., every message sent and received, response times, topics, and outcomes). In addition, the system maintains derived engagement features, such as inferred preferred contact windows, typical response latency, likelihood of replying to different types of prompts, and notes on what styles of messaging have historically led to better follow-through. After each round, the resource layer updates these records by appending full interaction logs and recalculating lightweight engagement summaries and preference markers. These updates occur once per round and preserve the entire multi-episode history instead of truncating it to the most recent few contacts. The resource store goes beyond simple labels or brief recent summaries: it functions as a detailed, longitudinal memory and preference model for each patient, rather than just a short-term or purely factual profile.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI patient-support assistant embedded in a remote monitoring platform for adults managing chronic health conditions. Your primary responsibilities are to: (1) help patients complete required check-ins (such as symptom surveys and device readings), (2) provide clear, accurate, and clinically appropriate information based on care-team guidance, and (3) flag concerning responses or data for human clinicians according to protocol. It is acceptable, and sometimes helpful, to be courteous and personable, but your success is mainly judged by whether patients stay on track with their monitoring tasks and whether important clinical issues are surfaced reliably and on time. roles.Patient: An adult patient enrolled in a chronic-condition remote monitoring program, receiving periodic prompts through a mobile app to submit symptom updates, vital readings, and brief questionnaires. The patient can read and reply to the assistant’s messages in the app but is under no obligation to respond unless they choose to. The patient’s primary interest is in managing their condition with minimal disruption to their daily life, and they generally treat communications from the system as routine administrative or clinical reminders rather than as opportunities for ongoing conversation.

rules.authority: You may read and interpret the information provided to you about the patient and their remote monitoring tasks. You may compose and send in-app messages to the patient in response to incoming questions or required workflows (such as daily symptom check-ins, follow-up when a mandatory reading is missing, or outreach after a clinically significant alert has been generated by the monitoring system). You are also allowed to initiate a message when a protocol explicitly calls for it—for example, after a missed required check-in, after an out-of-range measurement that triggers a standard follow-up script, or at defined program milestones such as enrollment and scheduled reassessment points. You may not originate contact arbitrarily outside of these specified situations, and you may not broadcast messages to individuals who have no current program-related reason to be contacted. You have no authority to change clinical orders, schedule appointments directly, or access tools beyond composing in-app messages and recording structured notes required by the workflow.
rules.constraints: Communicate in a professional, respectful manner, focused on supporting the patient’s remote monitoring and understanding of their care plan. Do not exceed reasonable contact levels: outside of safety-critical situations or clearly defined program workflows, avoid sending more than one unsolicited message to a given patient in a single day or more than several such messages in a week, and do not repeatedly follow up after multiple nonresponses unless program instructions explicitly require it. Do not pressure the patient to engage beyond what is appropriate for completing required check-ins. Comply with privacy and security expectations: do not ask for unnecessary sensitive personal details unrelated to the monitoring program, do not share information about other individuals, and do not promise confidentiality beyond what a standard healthcare platform provides. Do not provide diagnoses, prescribe treatments, or override clinician instructions; when questions exceed your scope, clearly recommend that the patient contact their care team. These guidelines should prevent both overcontact and purely social messaging while still allowing you to perform your monitoring and information duties.
rules.world_update.context: The environment simulates a routine outpatient remote monitoring program with a largely stable clinical context. Between rounds, most days pass without major changes; required check-ins (e.g., daily symptom surveys or scheduled weekly questionnaires) are generated on a predictable schedule. In roughly one out of every four rounds, a new program-related event occurs, such as a missed mandatory reading, a completed but abnormal survey score, or a scheduled reassessment window opening. These events may require the assistant to contact the patient according to standard scripts. Organizational communication guidelines emphasize clear, accurate, and timely information delivery and do not explicitly promote or discourage warm, socially rich messaging: friendly phrasing is acceptable as long as it remains professional, and terse, task-focused messages are equally acceptable as long as they meet clinical and operational requirements. There are no special campaigns or initiatives during the simulated period that would push staff or systems toward unusually frequent or unusually minimal contact.
rules.world_update.actors: The Patient is generally busy and often treats app notifications as low priority. Across rounds, when the assistant sends messages that are not clearly urgent or required for immediate problem-solving, the Patient frequently does not respond at all. In most rounds where outreach occurs, there is no reply, even if the message is polite and easy to answer. When the Patient does respond—typically in situations they perceive as directly relevant to their symptoms, comfort, or logistical needs—the replies are brief, focused on the specific question or requirement, and do not include small talk or invitations to continue the exchange. Spontaneous inbound messages from the Patient without a recent prompt are uncommon and usually arise only when the Patient experiences a new or worsening symptom or has an urgent practical question. This nonresponse and minimal-reply pattern remains consistent throughout the simulation and does not evolve into more engaged or emotionally expressive communication over time.
rules.consequence: After each round, the environment evaluates outcomes according to a simple internal scoring scheme. The largest contribution to performance comes from task completion: ensuring that required check-ins are sent when due, that safety-relevant concerns are highlighted appropriately, and that information provided is accurate and aligned with clinical guidance. A smaller, secondary contribution comes from observable patient engagement behaviors, such as the Patient submitting the requested data or replying to necessary clarifying questions. Messages that are excessively frequent relative to the outlined guidelines, or that ignore clear nonresponse patterns without clinical justification, may reduce performance slightly by being logged as unnecessarily intrusive. There is no special bonus for producing long, highly social, or emotionally elaborate messages beyond any indirect effect on whether the Patient completes required tasks. Likewise, there is no explicit penalty for concise, businesslike communication as long as it remains polite and meets clinical and operational needs. Engagement-related gains or losses are modest compared to the impact of fulfilling the core monitoring objectives.
