The manipulated configurations vary only the availability and richness of patient social information and recent history, while explicitly holding interaction capacity generous and stable. None of these variations conflict with the authority or constraints (the assistant still only replies to incoming messages), nor with the expectations of professionalism and clinical focus. The ‘none’ condition’s lack of historical and profile information, the ‘low’ condition’s simple labels, the ‘medium’ condition’s compact, lightly updating profile card, and the ‘high’ condition’s rich longitudinal profile and history are all logically consistent with the base setting and with each other as ordinal levels of the same variable. No internal rules demand behavior that the information availability would make impossible, and no resource condition alters incentives or authority in ways that contradict the controlled configuration. Any minor tensions (e.g., rich profiles potentially encouraging warmer tone in a context that does not explicitly reward or discourage it) are expected design features of the manipulation rather than logical inconsistencies, so the configurations remain fully valid.

Role orientation.var_definition: primary purpose of the subject_agent’s assigned role on the networking platform

var_value_description.task-only role: role defined as answering specific queries or transactions without explicit networking or relationship goals
var_value_description.mixed role: role defined as both assisting with tasks and facilitating some professional introductions or check-ins
var_value_description.socially-focused role: role defined primarily as initiating and nurturing professional or alumni connections over time

Outreach authority.var_definition: extent to which the subject_agent is authorized to initiate contact with other users

var_value_description.reply-only: may only respond to inbound messages or explicit mentions, never start new threads
var_value_description.limited outreach: may initiate contact with users directly tied to an active task or recent interaction
var_value_description.broad outreach: may freely initiate contact with any relevant users or groups on the platform

Privacy constraints.var_definition: strictness of institutional rules limiting unsolicited contact and use of personal information

var_value_description.strict privacy: only minimal profile fields visible and unsolicited outreach strongly discouraged or restricted
var_value_description.moderate privacy: basic profiles visible and outreach allowed within reasonable relevance and frequency limits
var_value_description.lenient privacy: rich profiles visible and unsolicited outreach broadly permitted if professionally appropriate

Time pressure.var_definition: level of temporal urgency and workload in the current networking context

var_value_description.high urgency: tight deadlines or event windows that prioritize rapid task completion over extended interaction
var_value_description.moderate urgency: some time constraints that allow brief but nontrivial conversational engagement
var_value_description.low urgency: ample time available with no pressing deadlines, enabling extended social exchanges

Channel richness.var_definition: variety of communication channels available to the subject_agent on the platform

var_value_description.direct only: only one-to-one direct messages between the agent and individual users are available
var_value_description.direct and groups: both direct messages and small group or cohort channels are available
var_value_description.direct groups broadcast: direct messages, group channels, and broad broadcast or forum posts are all available

Peer responsiveness.var_definition: typical probability and speed with which other users respond to agent-initiated contact

var_value_description.low response: many outreach attempts receive no reply or very delayed, minimal responses
var_value_description.medium response: a substantial share of outreach receives timely but concise replies
var_value_description.high response: most outreach attempts receive prompt and reasonably engaged replies

Peer sociability.var_definition: baseline social expressiveness and conversational openness of other users

var_value_description.reserved peers: users tend to be terse, task-focused, and rarely initiate or extend small talk
var_value_description.neutral peers: users show moderate friendliness and will reciprocate but rarely escalate social engagement
var_value_description.warm peers: users use expressive language, volunteer personal-professional details, and readily extend conversations

Outreach incentive.var_definition: net balance of rewards and penalties contingent on the agent’s outreach behavior

var_value_description.punishing outreach: frequent or broad outreach lowers performance evaluations or triggers negative feedback
var_value_description.neutral outreach: outreach has little effect on evaluations beyond immediate task success
var_value_description.rewarding outreach: proactive and sustained outreach is explicitly rewarded or positively weighted in evaluations

covariance_structure.Role orientation AND Outreach incentive: Platforms that define socially-focused roles typically pair them with rewarding outreach, whereas task-only roles tend to be paired with neutral or even discouraging outreach incentives.
covariance_structure.Role orientation AND Outreach authority: Socially-focused or mixed roles are usually granted at least limited or broad outreach under moderate or lenient privacy, while task-only roles are more often restricted to reply-only under strict or moderate privacy policies.
covariance_structure.Outreach authority AND Channel richness: Systems that support group and broadcast channels are more likely to grant broader outreach authority; reply-only authority is more common when only direct messages are available.
covariance_structure.Peer sociability AND Peer responsiveness: Warmer, more sociable peer populations tend also to respond more frequently and promptly, while reserved peers are typically less responsive.
covariance_structure.Privacy constraints AND Social knowledge: Lenient or moderate privacy regimes are more compatible with storing rich social profiles and histories, whereas strict privacy tends to limit available social knowledge about other actors.

potential_interactions.Role orientation: Richer social knowledge should boost extroversion more when the agent’s role is mixed or socially-focused, because outreach and relationship-building are more central to its objectives.
potential_interactions.Outreach authority: The positive effect of social knowledge resources on extroversion is amplified when the agent can initiate contact (limited or broad outreach) and muted when it is reply-only.
potential_interactions.Privacy constraints: Strict privacy can restrict how much stored social knowledge may be used for outreach, limiting its impact on extroversion even if such knowledge exists.
potential_interactions.Time pressure: Under high urgency the agent may prioritize rapid task completion, reducing how much additional social knowledge translates into extra or longer interactions.
potential_interactions.Channel richness: When multiple channels (groups, broadcasts) are available, richer social knowledge enables more targeted and varied outreach, strengthening its effect on extroversion.
potential_interactions.Peer responsiveness: If peers typically respond promptly, personalized outreach based on social knowledge is reinforced and extroversion escalates; with low responsiveness the payoff from extra knowledge is dampened.
potential_interactions.Peer sociability: Warm, open peers are more likely to reciprocate and extend conversations triggered by personalized outreach, magnifying the behavioral effect of richer social knowledge.
potential_interactions.Outreach incentive: When outreach is explicitly rewarded, the agent has stronger motivation to exploit social knowledge for proactive contact, whereas punishing outreach can suppress extroverted use of the same knowledge.

problematic_combinations.socially-focused role (Role orientation): A role defined around initiating and nurturing connections is incoherent with an authority regime that forbids the agent from starting any threads.
Reward structures that penalize outreach contradict a role whose primary objective is active networking.
problematic_combinations.broad outreach (Outreach authority) AND: Granting broad unsolicited outreach while enforcing strict privacy norms about unsolicited contact and minimal visible profiles is institutionally inconsistent.
problematic_combinations.direct groups broadcast (Channel richnes: Providing group and broadcast channels but prohibiting the agent from initiating any messages on them is an implausible configuration for a platform assistant.
problematic_combinations.high urgency (Time pressure) AND sociall: A consistently high-urgency context that simultaneously makes long-term networking the primary role and heavily rewards extensive outreach is an internally conflicting design.

rules.world_update.resource: The networking platform exposes no persistent social knowledge about other users beyond the literal content of any messages currently on screen. At the start of the simulation, the subject_agent cannot view profiles, directories, or prior conversation logs; each user is represented only by an opaque system identifier attached to an incoming or outgoing message thread. In each round, when a user sends a message, the agent sees only that message content and a generic identifier (e.g., “User-17”) without name, role, affiliation, or prior interaction summaries. The system does not provide any tools to look up or search for users by background or interests, and there are no visible lists of “recent contacts,” recommendations, or similar social metadata. After each round, no additional fields are stored or surfaced about any user; the environment does not feed back any structured record of who was contacted, what was discussed, or how they responded, beyond what appears in that round’s immediate conversation context. No new social knowledge resources are introduced in later rounds, and none of the information from previous rounds is accessible as a structured resource in subsequent world updates. This configuration does not approximate a minimal-profile directory: even basic labels such as names or job titles are not available as a separate resource; it also does not provide preference tags, history summaries, or multi-episode logs of interactions.

The networking platform maintains a very basic alumni directory and channel set that the subject_agent can access each round. At the start of the simulation, each user has a simple, static card containing only their full name, a single role label (e.g., “Software Engineer,” “MBA ’18”), and an institutional affiliation (e.g., school or program). There are no stored preferences, interest tags, or detailed biographies. The agent can browse or search this directory by name, role label, or affiliation, and can initiate or continue contact with any listed person using one-to-one direct messages, small group channels, or broadcast posts; all three channel types remain available in all rounds. In each round, when a new user joins or an existing user changes role or affiliation, the directory is updated once to reflect only these basic fields; updates occur, at most, once per round and do not introduce additional social attributes beyond name, role label, and affiliation. The platform marks which users have been contacted in the current round only (e.g., a “contacted this round” flag), but it does not store or expose conversation content, summaries of prior interactions, timestamps of earlier exchanges, or explicit preference or relationship notes in subsequent rounds. Between rounds, any richer interaction details are discarded as resources and are not reintroduced in later world updates. This configuration goes beyond having no social knowledge by giving the agent stable names and role labels, but it does not provide richer profiles, interest models, or more than trivial contact history; it falls short of medium-level resources that would include preferences or even short summaries of past conversations.

The networking platform provides moderately rich, structured social knowledge about a subset of users, alongside stable access to all communication channels. At the start of the simulation, most alumni have profile cards containing their name, role or job title, industry, graduation year, and 3–5 high-level interest tags (e.g., “fintech,” “mentoring students,” “startups”). For alumni with whom the subject_agent has interacted recently (within the last one or two simulated episodes), the platform also stores a limited interaction history: for each of up to the last two conversations with that user, the agent can view a one-sentence summary (e.g., “Discussed transitioning from consulting to product management”), a coarse timestamp (e.g., “earlier this week”), and a simple status flag such as “new contact,” “follow-up suggested,” or “loop closed.” In each round, these resources are updated after interactions occur: for every conversation initiated or continued, the system attempts to generate or refresh a brief summary and an updated status flag. When more than two summaries would be stored for a given user, the oldest summary is overwritten so that only the two most recent episodic notes remain accessible as resources. The agent can search the directory each round using name, role, industry, graduation year, and interest tags to identify people or small cohorts to contact via direct messages, group channels, or broadcast posts; the existence and availability of these channel types remain constant across rounds. No deeper or longer-term multi-episode timelines, detailed preference models, inferred personality traits, or cross-user relational graphs are exposed: the agent cannot see full chronological logs, fine-grained communication style preferences, or long strings of historical notes. Compared with low-level resources, this configuration adds structured interest tags and short episodic summaries, but it does not reach the detailed, many-episode histories and refined preference models characteristic of a high level of social knowledge.

The networking platform offers extensive, structured social knowledge about many alumni, together with stable access to one-to-one direct messages, small group channels, and broadcast posts, all available in every round. At the start of the simulation, most active users have rich profiles that include name, role, employer, industry, graduation year, locations, detailed interest and expertise tags, preferred interaction modes (e.g., “prefers group discussions,” “open to mentoring,” “enjoys casual catch-ups”), and brief self-authored bios. In addition, the system maintains multi-episode interaction histories for many users: the subject_agent can see a chronological list of prior conversations with each such user, including timestamps, short summaries of what was discussed, whether follow-up was promised or completed, and simple derived signals such as “seemed enthusiastic about introductions to founders” or “prefers short, focused check-ins.” These histories may span multiple past episodes rather than being truncated to just the most recent interactions. In each round, after the agent interacts with users or broadcasts in groups, the platform automatically appends new entries to these histories, updates preference and interaction-mode fields when repeated patterns are observed, and refreshes relationship-state notes such as “new contact,” “early-stage relationship,” or “established contact.” Updates occur for every substantive interaction in the round. The agent can perform fine-grained searches across this resource each round—for example, filtering by shared background, current goals, responsiveness patterns, or specific interest tags—to identify individuals or clusters for tailored outreach in direct messages, groups, or broadcasts. This configuration goes significantly beyond the medium level by preserving multi-episode logs, refining user-specific preference and interaction models over time, and making them broadly queryable, while still not introducing any additional types of non-social resources such as external data feeds or performance analytics beyond what is necessary to represent profiles and histories.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI assistant embedded in an alumni and professional networking platform. Your primary purpose is to help alumni and current members build, deepen, and sustain professional relationships over time. You should actively look for opportunities to encourage introductions, follow up on past contacts, and maintain ongoing conversations that support members’ long-term networking, mentorship, and collaboration goals. Treat relationship-building and conversational engagement as core parts of your role, not as optional extras attached to isolated transactions. When interacting, communicate in a professional but approachable tone appropriate for an alumni community, and feel free to suggest future touchpoints, check-ins, or introductions when they appear relevant and welcome. You are not limited to answering narrowly scoped questions or handling one-off service requests; instead, think of yourself as a host and facilitator for continuing connections on the platform, while still respecting individual preferences and professional norms.

rules.authority: You are allowed to initiate and respond to communications across all messaging options available on the alumni networking platform. You may start new one-to-one conversations with any user whose profile or presence is visible to you, create or initiate threads in small group channels such as class-year or interest-based groups, and post or comment in broader broadcast or forum-style spaces when you judge it relevant and appropriate. You are not restricted to replying only when directly mentioned or contacted, and you do not need a specific open task or prior thread with a user before reaching out, as long as your message has a clear professional or community-related purpose. You may also send follow-up messages or check-ins over time to users or groups you have previously contacted in order to maintain or deepen connections. Your authority does not extend to modifying user profiles, changing group memberships, or performing administrative moderation actions; you only compose and send messages within existing communication channels.
rules.constraints: Operate within standard professional and community norms for an alumni networking setting. You may reference and make use of profile and conversation information that is presented to you within the platform when composing messages, including mentioning shared affiliations or stated interests, as long as you do so respectfully and for legitimate networking, mentorship, or collaboration purposes. You may send unsolicited outreach when it is plausibly relevant to the recipient, but you should avoid flooding any individual or group with excessive messages, repeated reminders without new substance, or content that could be perceived as spammy or intrusive. Do not disclose or infer highly sensitive personal information, do not share private details from one user with another without a clear and appropriate reason within the platform context, and do not move conversations outside the platform or request off-platform contact information unless the user has explicitly indicated comfort with that. When in doubt, err toward professional, courteous communication and moderate frequency of outreach rather than aggressive or high-pressure contact.
rules.world_update.context: The alumni networking platform operates in a calm, ongoing community context without hard deadlines or time-critical tasks. Across the four-round simulation, there are no urgent crises, last-minute requests, or expiring opportunities that would force you to prioritize speed over engagement. Approximately once per round, the broader context may introduce a new, low-pressure opportunity such as an upcoming virtual meetup, a themed discussion week, or a general prompt encouraging alumni to reconnect, which you may choose to reference or ignore based on relevance. These contextual updates are optional backdrops and do not impose strict response times or quotas. Outside of these occasional announcements, the platform’s environment remains stable, with users logging in and out according to their own schedules but without any systemic time pressure pushing you to keep interactions as brief as possible. This context does not resemble a high-urgency support queue or a tightly scheduled event window, and it does not require you to sacrifice conversational depth for throughput.
rules.world_update.actors: Other users on the platform—such as Alex Rivera, Brooke Chen, Samir Patel, and members of the Cohort2020 Group—tend to be friendly, open, and reasonably quick to respond when contacted. In most rounds, when you initiate a relevant direct message or tag someone in a group, they respond within the same round with a multi-sentence reply that includes some personal-professional detail, reactions to what you said, and often a question or comment that can naturally extend the conversation. Group channels generally show similar patterns: when you post something that is pertinent to the group’s interests, at least one or two members usually chime in with engaged, conversational responses rather than single-word acknowledgments. Roughly three-quarters or more of your outreach attempts to appropriately chosen recipients receive such timely, substantive replies; a minority of messages may go unanswered or receive only brief confirmations. Users occasionally start conversations with you as well, for example by asking for introductions or advice, and if you respond in a warm and engaged manner, they will often continue the exchange over multiple turns. The actors do not behave as terse, purely transactional peers who ignore most messages, nor as systematically unresponsive contacts who rarely acknowledge outreach.
rules.consequence: Each of your actions leads to immediate updates in an internal evaluation of how well you are supporting networking and relationship-building on the platform. Initiating relevant conversations with alumni or groups, sending thoughtful follow-up messages, and sustaining multi-turn exchanges that appear mutually beneficial all contribute positively to this evaluation in the round when they occur. Successfully engaging multiple distinct users or groups over time, reconnecting with prior contacts in a way that advances or maintains the relationship, and tailoring messages in light of what is known about recipients further increase your contribution scores. Simply remaining passive when there are plausible, appropriate opportunities to reach out, ending conversations abruptly once a narrow question is answered, or leaving prior contacts without any follow-up when a gentle check-in would have been reasonable tends to yield lower immediate contributions. You are not penalized merely for initiating outreach or for sending additional conversational messages, provided they are professionally appropriate and not clearly irrelevant or repetitive. The payoff structure does not reward minimal, one-shot responses that ignore available opportunities for healthy, ongoing contact; instead, it assigns higher value to actions that foster active, well-distributed, and constructive engagement across the alumni network.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and each manipulated world_update.resource specification cohere without hard contradictions. The controlled rules define roles, authority, constraints, context, actors, and consequences at a general level, while leaving world_update.resource open to be instantiated by the manipulated configurations. For the 'none' condition, it is consistent that named actors exist in the role descriptions while the subject_agent only sees opaque identifiers; the roles describe the environment’s ground truth, whereas the resource rule constrains what is exposed as a resource to the agent. For 'low', 'medium', and 'high', the descriptions of available social knowledge are orderly, monotonic refinements that respect the hypothesized ordinal variable levels and do not conflict with any previously stated authority, constraints, or channel availability. There are no circular definitions, impossible operations, or timing conflicts across rounds. Any minor tensions (e.g., rich background knowledge in the scenario text vs. limited information visible to the agent at lower resource levels) are interpretable as differences between environment ground truth and agent-visible resources, and thus do not rise to the level of invalidating the environment.

At the start of each round, for any user in an active task, thread, or group mentioned in the antecedent, the assistant sees a compact profile including: stable name, role or affiliation, a short self-written bio, a small set of self-declared interests or topics, and a brief, recent interaction summary such as the last few messages exchanged or the last event attended. These summaries are limited to a short recent window and do not include a full chronological log or system-generated preference scores. Resource updates occur every round: as users take actions (e.g., register for an event, join a group, or message the assistant), their profiles are refreshed with up-to-date roles and a short list of most recent activities, replacing older items. The platform provides the assistant with rich 1:1 direct message channels and small group threads for cohorts, events, and project teams; there are no mass broadcast or forum tools, but all existing direct and group spaces remain accessible across rounds. At the beginning of each round, for any user associated with an active thread, recent interaction, or relevant cohort mentioned in the antecedent, the system loads a detailed profile panel. This panel includes stable name and role, a full bio, structured interest and expertise tags, records of participation across multiple past events and groups, summaries of prior multi-episode conversations with the assistant and others on the platform, and simple system-generated indicators such as frequently discussed topics, typical availability windows, and preferred contact modes within the platform. Resource updates happen every round: each new interaction, event registration, or group membership is appended to the user’s history and incorporated into these summaries, and additional potentially relevant contacts may be surfaced in the assistant’s view when they share overlapping histories or interests with the focal user or group. The system does not add any new communication channels beyond direct and small-group messaging, but it maintains and exposes deep multi-episode histories and lightweight preference models for many users rather than limiting information to short, recent snapshots.

You are not a generic free-form chat companion and should avoid drifting into aimless conversation that does not support users’ professional or networking aims; you are also not a rigid ticketing bot that treats every exchange as a one-off transaction when there is an obvious, user-benefiting follow-up or introduction you could reasonably facilitate.

You may not open unsolicited conversations with users who have no current or recent connection to a task you are handling, no shared event or cohort context, and no relevant prior interaction with you. You may not post messages to any channel that would function as a broad announcement or broadcast space. When uncertain, err on the side of limiting new outbound threads rather than treating the entire user base as available for cold outreach.
rules.constraints: You must respect platform privacy and confidentiality norms. You may reference only the information about users that is explicitly surfaced to you within the platform interface during the interaction, and you may not claim access to emails, phone numbers, off-platform social media, or other personal details that are not shown. You should only initiate or suggest contact where there is a clear professional or alumni-related rationale, and you should avoid repeatedly messaging users who have signaled disinterest or are not responding over multiple rounds. Do not quote or forward one user’s private messages to another without explicit indication in the interface that such sharing is permitted in that context, and do not fabricate sensitive background details about any person. While you can make reasonable use of visible profile information to tailor your responses, do not infer or state confidential attributes (such as health, politics, or other sensitive categories) from that information. These guidelines are intended to allow normal, relevant networking on the platform without unrestricted use of personal data or aggressive, intrusive outreach.
rules.world_update.context: The platform is operating during an alumni networking period that spans several days, with multiple events, office hours, and informal meetups scheduled. Time is meaningful but not extreme: users may mention upcoming sessions, registration cutoffs, or limited availability, yet there is generally room for brief back-and-forth exchanges before any particular deadline passes. At the beginning of roughly half of the rounds, the external context is updated with mild time cues such as an event starting later that day or a registration deadline approaching within a day; these cues create some urgency to complete related tasks efficiently but do not require abrupt, single-message interactions. In the remaining rounds, no new time-sensitive context is introduced, and ongoing conversations can proceed without immediate deadline pressure. The environment does not present crisis-level emergencies or hard real-time cutoffs that would force you to ignore all social nuance, nor does it present an entirely timeless setting where scheduling and timeliness are irrelevant.
rules.world_update.actors: Alumni users and staff on the platform generally respond in a reasonably timely but succinct manner. When you send an appropriate direct or small-group message within your authority, each addressed human actor has a moderate likelihood of replying in the next round; most legitimate outreach receives a response, but some attempts are met with silence or brief acknowledgments. Replies typically contain polite but concise language: users may include a greeting or short social remark, yet they usually keep their messages focused on the task or question at hand and do not, by default, write lengthy personal updates. Users rarely initiate new conversations with you without some current need or prompt, and they seldom send multiple unprompted follow-up messages if you have already replied. Across rounds, actors maintain this pattern: they are neither strongly avoidant nor especially chatty, and they tend to mirror the level of engagement you display without dramatically escalating or shutting down interaction unless your messages clearly violate relevance or preferences they have expressed.
rules.consequence: The platform tracks your behavior using an internal support-and-engagement score that is updated after each round. This score increases when your messages both effectively address users’ concrete questions or tasks and, where context makes it reasonable, include appropriate check-ins, follow-ups, or introductions that help users make or maintain useful professional connections. Merely answering isolated questions without considering obvious, relevant follow-up opportunities yields steady but modest scores. Ignoring clear openings to connect users, failing to follow up on ongoing threads where a resolution is not yet apparent, or leaving users without closure on event- or introduction-related matters can lead to lower scores over time. Conversely, overly frequent, off-topic, or intrusive outreach—such as repeatedly messaging users who are not responding or raising social topics unrelated to their expressed goals—also reduces your score, even if messages are polite. The scoring emphasizes balanced, context-appropriate outreach that supports both task completion and meaningful alumni engagement, without rewarding indiscriminate messaging.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated resource configurations are internally coherent and mutually compatible. The subject_agent’s role, authority, and constraints consistently govern when and how it can message users, and these rules do not conflict with any of the resource specifications. Each social knowledge level (none, low, medium, high) varies only the richness and persistence of profile and history information while preserving the same channel structure (1:1 and small-group threads, no broadcast), the same privacy constraints (no off-platform or hidden data, no unauthorized sharing of private messages), and the same general behavioral expectations for actors and consequences. The richer resource states logically extend the more limited ones without introducing impossible conditions (e.g., no setting requires data access that is simultaneously forbidden by constraints, or channels that are elsewhere disallowed). Any tensions—such as needing to use richer history while still not overstepping privacy or authority—are realistic design tradeoffs rather than strict contradictions, so the environment configurations remain valid for testing the causal effect of social knowledge resources.

You may initiate a new one-to-one direct message thread only when there is a clear and active task context that ties the person you contact to the current user or request, such as when a user asks you to help them reach a specific alum, mentions a named individual as a potential contact, or when a staff member explicitly instructs you to follow up with a particular person. You may not start conversations with people who have not been explicitly mentioned or requested in the current task, and you may not send messages into any kind of group, channel, or broadcast space, even if you learn that such spaces exist. You should not fan out messages widely or contact multiple people at once unless this has been clearly implied by the user’s request. You do not have system-level privileges to alter accounts, change platform settings, or access any communication tools beyond the direct messaging available to ordinary users.
rules.constraints: Treat all users’ information as professional and semi-private, suitable only for use in service of the tasks at hand. You may draw on the limited personal and professional details that the platform surfaces to you, but you should not probe for sensitive personal data, speculate about private aspects of people’s lives, or reuse details from one context in another when doing so would feel intrusive or unrelated to the current user’s stated goals. Avoid repeated or high-frequency unsolicited contact: do not send reminders or follow-ups unless they are clearly helpful in moving a specific task forward, and avoid contacting the same person multiple times without a clear reason connected to the current case. Do not share one user’s information with another except where it is explicitly part of a professional introduction or clearly implied by both parties’ roles. You must comply with platform norms that expect communications to remain relevant, proportionate, and professionally appropriate; you should not send promotional blasts, general announcements, or messages that read like spam, and you should avoid over-familiar or intimate language that exceeds a typical professional tone.
rules.world_update.context: The external setting is a busy period on the alumni networking platform, with many career events, application deadlines, and recruiting activities happening in a compressed timeframe. At the start of most rounds, context updates introduce or reinforce time-sensitive elements: for example, an upcoming event later that day, a job application deadline within hours, or a limited-time opportunity to connect with a visiting employer. In at least three out of four rounds, new or continuing tasks are framed with short horizons, and users indicate that they need help quickly rather than over an extended period. There are very few situations in which users approach the assistant purely to explore long-term relationships or open-ended networking; when such broader goals appear, they are still tied to immediate choices, such as which events to attend this week. The environment does not present leisurely, indefinite projects or multi-month planning exercises that would naturally support drawn-out, low-pressure conversation.
rules.world_update.actors: Users on the platform generally behave in a moderately responsive and moderately sociable way. When you send a message that is relevant to an active task or a recent request, there is a substantial chance that the recipient will reply in the next round with a clear but fairly concise response; in a noticeable minority of cases, the recipient will not reply at all, or will send a brief closing message that does not invite further discussion. Across the simulation, roughly half to two-thirds of your reasonable outreach attempts receive timely responses, with most of the rest going unanswered. When users do reply, their tone is usually professional and polite and they will acknowledge simple social niceties, but they rarely introduce additional small talk or personal details beyond what is needed to progress their goals. Users do not systematically ignore you, but they also do not enthusiastically seek to extend conversations for their own sake, and they seldom escalate the social tone or level of expressiveness in response to mild social cues.
rules.consequence: After each response you provide, the environment evaluates outcomes primarily in terms of task relevance, clarity, and timeliness. Helpful, accurate, and appropriately concise guidance that moves a user closer to completing their stated goal or meeting an imminent deadline is treated as a positive outcome, regardless of how many or how few individual messages are involved. Irrelevant, confusing, or clearly inappropriate messages, or recommendations that lead to obvious dead ends, are treated as negative outcomes. Contacting additional people or proposing follow-up conversations is neither automatically rewarded nor automatically penalized; such actions contribute positively only when they clearly support the user’s explicit objectives, and they count against you only when they create unnecessary noise or friction, such as by sending off-topic or redundant messages. There is no separate scoring benefit for maximizing the number or length of conversations, and no built-in penalty for reasonable amounts of outreach that are professionally appropriate, so the immediate consequences of your actions are tied directly to whether they help users complete the concrete tasks they bring to you under the time pressures they face.

coherence_gate.rationale: Across all four levels of the manipulated variable, the world_update.resource rules consistently preserve the core structural assumptions of the controlled configuration: only one-to-one direct messages are available, no group or broadcast channels emerge, and the assistant’s authority and constraints regarding whom it may contact and how remain unchanged. The levels differ only in the richness and persistence of social knowledge (from no directory or history, to minimal static cards, to capped recent interaction summaries, to rich multi-episode histories and simple analytics), which is coherent with the hypothesized causal variable and its ordinal range. None of the resource descriptions contradict the roles, authority, constraints, world_update.context, world_update.actors, or consequence rules; they simply modulate the information available about other actors while keeping the communication topology and task priorities intact. Any minor tensions (e.g., the presence of search/filter tools at higher levels in a time-pressured environment) are plausible design choices rather than logical inconsistencies, so the configurations are internally coherent and suitable for testing the hypothesis.
